findings.exact_estimate: Multivariate % difference = –37.3% (95% CI: –46.4%, –26.5%), p < 0.001 (adjusted for number of people in household, household monthly income per capita, and religion); Univariate % difference = –38.2%, p < 0.001; N = 593 households (283 notified, 310 non-notified). Translates to ~12 fewer LPCD based on notified median.
findings.exposure_and_reference: Legal status of household: Non-notified neighbourhood (Indira Nagar, legally unrecognized/excluded, n = 310) vs. Notified neighbourhood (Matangrushi Nagar, legally recognized, Ref, n = 283)
findings.finding_label: Primary headline model: Multivariate linear regression of household water quantity (log-transformed LPCD)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Water quantity used by households in litres per capita per day (LPCD, log-transformed and exponentiated to % difference); higher numerical values = BETTER household water access/consumption
findings.table_or_page: Table 3, PDF Page 15 (and text PDF Page 12)

findings.exact_estimate: Adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 3.4 (reported in text as '3.4 higher adjusted odds of using ⩽20 LPCD compared with notified households'; full table in online Supplementary Appendix Table S1; bivariate proportion using ⩽20 LPCD: Non-notified 171/310 [55.2%] vs. Notified 82/283 [29.0%], p < 0.001); N = 593 households.
findings.exposure_and_reference: Legal status of household: Non-notified (n = 310) vs. Notified (Ref, n = 283)
findings.finding_label: Robustness model: Multivariate logistic regression of very low water consumption (⩽20 LPCD)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Household water use ⩽20 LPCD (WHO 'very high' health-risk threshold); higher numerical values / higher odds = WORSE household water access (severe water deprivation)
findings.table_or_page: PDF Page 12 (Section III.b) & PDF Page 14 (Table 2), citing Table S1

findings.exact_estimate: Unmediated total association = –38.2% LPCD; direct (unmediated residual) association = –23.4% LPCD after adjusting for mediators (primary/secondary water source, households sharing source, collection time, water cost, frequency/reliability), indicating 38.7% of the association is explained by mediating water service indicators (up to 50% in a more complex variation); N = 593 households.
findings.exposure_and_reference: Legal status of household: Non-notified vs. Notified (Ref)
findings.finding_label: Exploratory GSEM path analysis of log-transformed water quantity (LPCD)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Log-transformed water quantity in LPCD (expressed as % difference); higher numerical values = BETTER household water access
findings.table_or_page: PDF Page 12 (Section III.c) & Figure 3, PDF Page 16 (citing Table S2)

findings.exact_estimate: Median (IQR) LPCD: Notified 31.4 (17.6–51.7) vs. Non-notified 17.7 (10.7–34.1), Wilcoxon p < 0.0001 (13 LPCD lower on average per text p. 11). Days insufficient water in past 2 weeks (chi-squared p < 0.001): 0 days = Notified 114 (40.3%) vs. Non-notified 61 (19.7%); >10 days = Notified 11 (3.9%) vs. Non-notified 52 (16.8%). Not enough water from drinking source in past 2 weeks: Notified 61 (21.6%) vs. Non-notified 124 (40.0%), p < 0.001; N = 593.
findings.finding_label: Bivariate comparisons of water quantity and insufficiency indicators
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Median LPCD (higher = BETTER access); days of insufficient household water and insufficient drinking water in past 2 weeks (higher = WORSE access)
findings.table_or_page: Table 2, PDF Page 14 (and text PDF Page 11)

findings.exact_estimate: Primary mode (chi-squared p < 0.001): Water tap within home = Notified 28 (9.9%) vs. Non-notified 8 (2.6%); Water vendor hose = Notified 171 (60.4%) vs. Non-notified 149 (48.1%); Shared community tap/tank = Notified 26 (9.2%, generally municipal piped) vs. Non-notified 65 (21.0%, often brackish borewells per footnote b); Tanker truck = Notified 8 (2.8%) vs. Non-notified 22 (7.1%); Fetch from another community = Notified 7 (2.5%) vs. Non-notified 32 (10.3%). Secondary mode (p < 0.001): No need for secondary source = Notified 133 (47.0%) vs. Non-notified 108 (34.8%); Secondary tanker truck = Notified 18 (6.4%) vs. Non-notified 120 (38.7%); N = 593.
findings.finding_label: Bivariate comparisons of primary and secondary water access modes (infrastructure)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Categorical distribution of primary and secondary water sources (in-home tap and no secondary source needed = BETTER access; tanker truck, fetching from other communities, brackish borewells = WORSE access)

findings.exact_estimate: Other households sharing primary source (p < 0.001): 0–59 households = Notified 157 (55.5%) vs. Non-notified 78 (25.2%); 60+ households = Notified 102 (36.0%) vs. Non-notified 186 (60.0%). Time per trip in last week (p = 0.045): ⩾50 minutes = Notified 73 (25.8%) vs. Non-notified 107 (34.5%). Frequency water obtained in last week (p < 0.001): <3 times = Notified 75 (26.5%) vs. Non-notified 152 (49.0%); 7+ times = Notified 153 (54.1%) vs. Non-notified 115 (37.1%); N = 593.
findings.finding_label: Bivariate comparisons of water accessibility (crowding, collection time) and reliability (frequency)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Source crowding (60+ households) and trip time (⩾50 min) (higher = WORSE access); weekly frequency of obtaining water 7+ times (higher = BETTER reliability)

findings.exact_estimate: Median water cost (text p. 11): Notified 219 INR/1000L (USD 2.92) vs. Non-notified 407 INR/1000L (USD 5.42); categorical cost (Table 2, p < 0.001): <200 INR/1000L = Notified 121 (42.8%) vs. Non-notified 68 (21.9%); 400+ INR/1000L = Notified 74 (26.2%) vs. Non-notified 160 (51.6%). Percentage of monthly household income spent on water, median (IQR): Notified 9% (5–17) vs. Non-notified 11% (6–20), p = 0.01; N = 593.
findings.finding_label: Bivariate comparisons of water unit cost and household water expenditure burden (affordability)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Unit water cost (INR/1000L) and % of monthly household income spent on water; higher numerical values = WORSE affordability/access

findings.exact_estimate: Sanitation method (chi-squared p = 0.005): Open defecation = Notified 6 (2.1%) vs. Non-notified 14 (4.5%); Home toilet = Notified 17 (6.0%) vs. Non-notified 39 (12.6%); Pay community toilet = Notified 260 (91.9%) vs. Non-notified 257 (82.9%); N = 593.
findings.finding_label: Descriptive comparison of household sanitation method (background table)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Categorical sanitation method (open defecation = WORSE sanitation; pay community toilet / home toilet = BETTER sanitation, though unadjusted multi-category chi-squared test mixes higher open defecation and higher home toilet in non-notified)

findings.exact_estimate: Missed or late for work due to water collection in past 2 weeks: Notified 64/283 (22.6%) vs. Non-notified 94/310 (30.3%), p = 0.03 (N = 593). Child missed or late for school/tuition due to water collection in past 2 weeks (among households with children, N = 376): Notified 27 (16.4%) vs. Non-notified 24 (11.5%), p = 0.18 (null).
findings.finding_label: Downstream social impacts of water collection on work and school attendance
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Missed/late work or school due to water collection; higher numerical values = WORSE downstream social/economic impact

headline_result_summary: In a representative cross-sectional survey of 593 households across two adjacent neighbourhoods of the Mandala slum in Mumbai, India—Matangrushi Nagar (legally recognized / notified, n = 283) and Indira Nagar (legally unrecognized / non-notified, n = 310)—legal exclusion (non-notified status) was strongly and significantly associated with worse household water access across infrastructure, accessibility, reliability, quantity, and affordability. In the primary multivariate linear regression controlling for household size, per capita income, and religion (Table 3, p. 15), non-notified households consumed 37.3% fewer litres per capita per day (LPCD) than notified reference households (95% CI: –46.4% to –26.5%, p < 0.001; univariate –38.2%, p < 0.001; median 17.7 vs. 31.4 LPCD, p < 0.0001), and had 3.4 times higher adjusted odds of severe water deprivation (⩽20 LPCD) in multivariate logistic regression (p. 12). Non-notified households also had fewer in-home taps (2.6% vs. 9.9%, p < 0.001), greater crowding and collection times, lower supply frequency, higher median water unit cost (407 vs. 219 INR/1000L, p < 0.001), and higher median income share spent on water (11% vs. 9%, p = 0.01). NOTE ON EXPOSURE POLARITY: As modeled by the authors (exposure = Non-notified [legal exclusion] vs. Notified [Ref]), the headline direction is unfavorable_to_access (raw sign negative on LPCD). Equivalently, if a synthesis codes the exposure pole in reverse as legal recognition / slum notification (Notified vs. Non-notified), legal recognition is favorable_to_access.
specification_or_coding_pitfalls:
1. EXPOSURE POLE SYMMETRY (LEGAL EXCLUSION vs. LEGAL RECOGNITION): Throughout Table 3, Figure 3, and the logistic regression, the authors set 'Notified' (legally recognized) as the Reference group and estimate the effect of 'Non-notified' (legal exclusion). Thus, for Non-notified status, the raw sign on LPCD is negative (–37.3%) and the substantive access valence is unfavorable_to_access. If a synthesis instead defines the intervention positively as 'slum notification / legal tenure recognition' (Notified vs. Non-notified), the substantive direction flips to favorable_to_access. Reconcilers must align which pole of notification status is treated as the exposure.
2. OUTCOME POLARITY FLIPS ACROSS MODELS & TABLES: In the primary linear regression (Table 3), higher values (LPCD) mean BETTER access (raw sign negative: –37.3%). In the robustness logistic regression (p. 12, Table S1), the outcome is ⩽20 LPCD (severe deprivation), where higher odds mean WORSE access (raw sign positive: aOR = 3.4). Similarly, in Table 2, unit water cost (407 vs. 219 INR/1000L) and % income spent on water (11% vs. 9%) are positively signed for non-notified households because higher cost/burden means WORSE affordability. All point to the same substantive conclusion (non-notified worse off / notified better off).
3. COMMUNITY TAP QUALITY CONFOUND IN TABLE 2: A naive reading of 'Shared community water tap or tank' in Table 2 (21.0% in non-notified vs. 9.2% in notified) might look favorable to non-notified households, but Footnote b (p. 14) explicitly warns that community taps in the notified neighbourhood were generally municipal piped water connections, whereas taps in the non-notified neighbourhood were often borewells drawing brackish, poor-quality groundwater.
4. NEIGHBOURHOOD-LEVEL OPERATIONALIZATION OF LEGAL STATUS: Notification status in this study was defined at the neighbourhood level (Matangrushi Nagar = notified; Indira Nagar = non-notified) rather than verified via individual pre-2000 household documents, reflecting how aggregate water infrastructure is deployed in practice (Section I.c & IV, p. 4, 17).
5. RELIGION ATTENUATION & SANITATION NUANCE: Religion (Hindu/Buddhist vs. Muslim) is positively associated with LPCD in univariate regression (+29.0%, p < 0.001) but becomes null and slightly negative (–8.4%, 95% CI: –21.9% to 7.5%, p = 0.283) once household legal status is controlled for (Table 3). In Table 1 (p. 10), descriptive sanitation differs (p = 0.005) in mixed directions (non-notified has higher open defecation [4.5% vs. 2.1%] and lower community toilet use [82.9% vs. 91.9%], but higher home toilets [12.6% vs. 6.0%]). School absence due to water collection is null (p = 0.18, N = 376).
study_design: Cross-sectional representative household survey (March–May 2016) with GIS infrastructure mapping, analysed via bivariate tests (chi-squared, Wilcoxon), multivariate linear and logistic regression, and generalized structural equation modelling (GSEM) path analysis
unit_and_sample_size: Households in two neighbourhoods of the Mandala slum, Mumbai (Matangrushi Nagar [notified] and Indira Nagar [non-notified]); 600 randomly sampled from neighbourhood census, 7 excluded for missing water data; primary analytic N = 593 households (283 notified, 310 non-notified; N = 376 households with children for school-absence outcome)
